newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya flights return to normal after go-slow.
newsitem.headline: Kenya flights return to normal after go-slow.

text.p: Flights to and from Kenya returned to normal on Friday after police released six air traffic controllers who took part in a five-day go-slow, air controllers said.
"The six were released today and there are no delays any more. Everything is back to normal," an air traffic controller at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport told Reuters.
"The six were detained for taking part in an illegal strike but will not be charged and now it's all air controllers doing the work. The instructors who were here left this morning," he added.
Freight forwarders and major airlines confirmed flights were back to normal following five days of cancellations and delays.

The controller had said earlier many controllers had not turned up for work on Friday because they feared being arrested for signing a letter saying they wanted to contine the go-slow after the government declared the dispute resolved on Thursday.
He said air traffic control instructors had been brought in on Thursday morning to work instead of full-time controllers.

On Thursday, Labour Minister Philip Masinde announced an end to the five-day old dispute, in which the controllers demanded a 50-fold increase from what they said was a salary of only $90 a month each and benefits.

Air traffic controllers said they returned to normal working on Thursday after being assured that a commission's report on terms and conditions for government workers presented to President Daniel arap Moi on Wednesday would meet their demands.
They said they would wait two weeks to see what the government gave them and if they were not satisfied they would either launch another go-slow or some other type of action.

"The go-slow is definitely off. Planes are landing and taking off as normal," said a manager with Lufthansa Cargo. "We expect our next cargo flight from Frankfurt to Johannesburg and back with stops in Nairobi to go as normal on Sunday.

"We have a flight out tonight with 30 tonnes of flowers and vegetables for Amsterdam and London and we don't expect any problems," said an official with the Dutch-owned Flower Wings freight forwarders.
British Airways said it had not heard of any problems on Friday and expected its flight to London to leave as scheduled.

The airlines and air traffic controllers said a one-day general strike called by an opposition-backed alliance demanding constitutional reforms did not hamper airport operations though some cargo shipments had been cancelled in case of trouble.
The go-slow ended after foreign airlines and freight forwarders said they were increasingly concerned about safety at Nairobi with flights circling over the capital for hours waiting to land.

At least 40 airlines use Kenyan airports and landing and parking fees brings millions of dollars in annual revenue. The go-slow forced many airlines to cancel flights while others were delayed for up to 12 hours.
Airports at Nairobi, the coast city of Mombasa, Kisumu and the tourist resort of Malindi were hit hard by the dispute.
